Assault on the Control Room from Halo: CE is among the most memorable to me. The level is wonderfully paced: swapping between interior spaces which have the best opportunity for stealth in the game (with the sleeping grunts everywhere, it's fun trying to melee all of them without getting caught), and the wider exterior spaces where you're fighting alongside marines with plenty of vehicular combat.

I still clearly recall that first moment you step outside on the snowy ground, with marines pinned down amongst the trees, ghosts racing around and the mortar fire of a wraith raining down on them. And the first time you saddle up in a scorpion with a full crew of marines sitting on board, trying to keep them alive as you make your way across the valley. And the final push on the ziggurat structure. All these moments bookended by the quiet interior segments and their elevator rides.

Every Covenant enemy, drivable vehicle, and power weapon were present throughout the level, providing you with choices of approach in the exterior areas. The perfect Halo: CE level imo, although Halo and The Silent Cartographer were great as well with their slightly nonlinear approaches.

In Shadow of the Colossus there are a ton of beautiful areas, but there is one in particular that I loved to just hang out in with no purpose in mind, a rarity for me. More for what you do there than the level itself, Ikana Canyon in Majora's Mask always stuck with me. I wasn't old enough to be a parent when I first played, but something about rescuing the daughter from the dad who couldn't control his actions because of the mask stuck with me. Now, as a parent, it has a different meaning. The sadness from knowing your child was terrified of you and there was nothing you could do about it.

Yeah, thinking back on it, Majora's Mask was an unusually deep game for that system and era. There's a crapload of events, meanings and inferences that the intended audience of kids would only really take at face value. There's that, but there's also the whole deal with Lulu's eggs in terms of parental nightmares. Really, the game is stuffed full of the sort of stuff that makes adults sweat at night, alongside the usual nightmare fuel. Facing your own mortality, being separated from your loved ones, losing family, facing down an incoming catastrophe that nobody can do anything about...

Thinking about it, there's good reasons why that game is better regarded by some people compared to other games in the series. Intentionally or not, the game seems to be stuffed with these hidden meanings and deep events that really make you wonder if they were just making the game for their usual audience. Oh well then, time to look up some fan theories.

Not sure, I've been gaming for awhile. I'll give a few nominations.

The Revelation, Jak 3 (2004)

This is gonna be a spoiler, hell, this is gonna be a huge spoiler, so if you haven't played the Jak and Daxter trilogy to completion, don't read this paragraph.

The Other Revelation, Jak 3 (2004)

More spoilers:

Tutorial Island, Runescape (2006)

Runescape has gotta be one of the best experiences I've ever had in gaming. I recently got into playing oldschool—2007scape—on the servers Jagex is now hosting. It's not as good as it was back in the day because of some unnecessary changes, but still. Your character on the oldschool servers starts from scratch, which I love because you get to reexperience the game. Admittedly, I had since forgotten that exact moment when I first made my character way back in the day, which was an incredibly important moment in my gaming history because of how much time I sunk into that game. I started up the game, appeared in Tutorial Island and Newbie Melody started playing. At the same time, all of those memories came flooding back. It was so much nostalgia my eyes started watering.

Everywhere, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion (2006)

Can't say much about this nomination besides the fact that I loved pretty much every area in this game. I have yet to play a game that did such a wonderful job capturing the medieval fantasy aesthetic that Bethesda captured in Oblivion. Just roaming the vast, sprawling hills of Cyrodill while listening to the music of Jeremy Soule (Can you believe this game came out almost 10 years ago?). That level of immersion has only been topped just recently by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and the only reason I said "I have yet to play a game that did such a wonderful job..." was because CDPR was going for a different, dark aesthetic while Bethesda was going for a bit of a lighter one. There's no doubt in my mind, however, that CDPR could have done better than Bethesda had they gone for the same kind of aesthetic.

The SA-X Boss Fight, Metroid: Fusion (2002)

All of Metroid: Fusion in general was one of my favorite areas in any game, but if I were to choose a specific part in that game it would be finally defeating the SA-X. This isn't a spoiler because you know you'll have to fight it eventually. I remember the exact moment I delivered the killing blow, I threw my head back and yelled, "I DEFEATED X!" I was home sick that day and my mom called from the kitchen, "You don't sound very sick!" I also need to give an honorable mention to pretty much everything that happens after that boss fight, but the biggest moment was when I defeated the SA-X.

Paradise Plaza, Dead Rising 1 (2006)

Dead Rising is easily the best experience I've ever had in a zombie-related game. Out of every game, Dead Rising handled the zombies the best. The zombies were dangerous, not because they had superhuman strength, special abilities, or even competence. The only thing the zombies had was numbers. The zombies in Dead Rising, as that loud fat guy said, "are stupid and slow." Dead Rising never introduced any sort of gimmick that gave zombies special powers or anything like that; zombies were zombies, and they remained zombies for the duration of the game. That being said, the Paradise Plaza is one of my favorite areas in any game because it was the main area.

Assault on the Control Room, Halo 1. Long level, lots of vehicles (including tanks) no Flood. Some long range sniping, some sneaking melee hits where you can take down a room full of 20 enemies silently if you are good enough.
The Silent Cartographer from the first Halo. God, I loved landing on that beach, clearing it and then heading into the facility. I played it over and over again.
Outset Island from Wind Waker. One of my favorite part of Wind Waker was exploring it at the beginning of the game.
